l: Amaziah's death by conspiracy, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Amaziah's death resulted from his turning away from the LORD: a conspiracy arose in Jerusalem, he fled to Lachish, conspirators pursued and killed him, and his body was returned by horses and buried with his fathers.

l: Uzziah, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Uzziah is a king of Judah, son of Amaziah and Jechiliah of Jerusalem, who becomes king at sixteen and reigns fifty-two years. He does right in the LORD's eyes and prospers while seeking God, winning military victories, receiving Ammonite tribute, rebuilding Eloth, fortifying Jerusalem, farming extensively, and equipping a large army. His fame reaches Egypt. Once strong, his heart is lifted up; he enters the temple to burn incense, angers at the priests' rebuke, and is struck with leprosy. He lives in a separate house, cut off from the temple, until death. Buried in the kings' burial field, he is succeeded by Jotham; Isaiah chronicles his reign.

l: priests (the eighty priests with Azariah), The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Eighty valiant priests of the LORD, descended from Aaron and consecrated to burn incense, follow Uzziah in with Azariah, resist him as a trespasser, see his leprosy, and swiftly expel him.

l: leprosy, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: afflicts Uzziah [on his forehead, struck by the LORD] Leprosy breaks out on Uzziah's forehead while he is angry with the priests, holding a censer beside the altar of incense. It is described as a strike from the LORD, and it leaves him a leper until his death, living in a separate house and buried apart in the kings' field because "He is a leper."

l: Uzziah's trespass in the temple, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Uzziah, grown strong and proud, corruptly enters the LORD's temple to burn incense on the altar. Azariah and eighty priests oppose him, saying it belongs to Aaron's consecrated sons; he persists in anger, is struck with leprosy, and loses his role.

l: Jotham, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Jotham was a king of Judah who succeeded his father Uzziah at age twenty-five and reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem. His mother was Jerushah, daughter of Zadok, and his son was Ahaz. He did right in the LORD's eyes but did not enter the temple. He built the temple's upper gate, the wall of Ophel, and cities, fortresses and towers in Judah, and defeated Ammon's king. He grew mighty by ordering his ways before God, and was buried in David's city.

l: Ahaz, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Ahaz was king of Judah, son and successor of Jotham, who began reigning at twenty and ruled sixteen years in Jerusalem. He did evil, unlike David: following Israel's kings, making molten images for the Baals, burning his children, and sacrificing at high places. He sought Assyria's help with temple treasure, but it failed him. He also sacrificed to Damascus's gods, cut up the temple vessels, shut the LORD's house, and built altars throughout Judah. He died and was buried in Jerusalem, not in the kings' tombs; his son Hezekiah succeeded him.

l: children of Ammon, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: pays tribute from Ammon [to Jotham for three years] The king of the children of Ammon fought with Jotham and was prevailed against. The children of Ammon then gave Jotham one hundred talents of silver, ten thousand cors of wheat and ten thousand cors of barley in that year, and the same amount in the second and third years.

l: Jotham's reign, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: has_duration 16 years Jotham's reign lasted sixteen years in Jerusalem, beginning when he was twenty-five. It was marked by right conduct in the LORD's eyes, building projects on the temple's upper gate, the Ophel wall, and cities, fortresses and towers in Judah, though the people still acted corruptly. The rest of his acts and wars are said to be written in the book of the kings of Israel and Judah, and it ended with his death and Ahaz's accession.

l: war with Ammon, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: A war between Jotham and the king of the children of Ammon; Jotham prevailed, and the Ammonites then paid yearly tribute of silver, wheat and barley for three years.

l: gods of Damascus, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Ahaz sacrificed to the gods of Damascus, reasoning that they had helped the kings of Syria who defeated him. The text says they instead became the ruin of him and of all Israel.

l: Pekah, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: is_son_of Remaliah Pekah the son of Remaliah killed 120,000 valiant men in Judah in one day. The text attributes this to Judah having forsaken the LORD, the God of their fathers.

l: captives of Judah, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: About 200,000 women, sons, and daughters of Judah were carried off to Samaria by Israel, along with plunder. After Oded's intervention, named Ephraimite men clothed, shod, fed, anointed them, carried the feeble on donkeys, and brought them to their brothers at Jericho, the city of palm trees.

l: Oded, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: is_a prophet of the LORD [in Samaria] Oded, a prophet of the LORD in Samaria, went out to meet the returning army and told them that Judah's defeat came from the LORD's anger and that their own rage had reached heaven. He told them to send back the captives from their brothers, warning of the LORD's fierce wrath. The armed men then left the captives and plunder.

l: Tilgath-pilneser, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Tilgath-pilneser, king of Assyria, answered Ahaz's call for help but troubled him instead of strengthening him, despite Ahaz paying him with temple and royal treasure.

l: Hezekiah, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Hezekiah is a king of Judah, son of Ahaz and Abijah's child, who begins to reign at twenty-five and rules twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. He does right in the LORD's eyes, following David his father, and is described as good, right and faithful, seeking his God with all his heart and prospering. In his first year he opens and repairs the temple doors, has the priests and Levites cleanse the house, and leads the offerings and singing. He sends couriers with letters to all Israel and Judah, including Ephraim and Manasseh, to keep the Passover in Jerusalem, after taking counsel with his princes. He prays for the unclean, and the LORD listens. He appoints priests and Levites into divisions, provides the king's portion for burnt offerings, commands the people to give the portions due, and has rooms prepared and overseers appointed. He removes high places and altars so worship is at one altar. Facing Sennacherib, he stops the springs, redirects Gihon, repairs the wall, strengthens Millo, makes weapons, sets captains and encourages the people, praying with Isaiah. After the deliverance he is exalted in the sight of all nations and gains exceedingly great riches from God, with treasuries, storehouses, cities, flocks and herds. He falls ill and is given a sign, becomes proud and brings wrath, then humbles himself; God tests him over the Babylonian ambassadors. He dies and is buried at the ascent to the tombs of the sons of David, and his son Manasseh succeeds him. His acts are recorded in the book of the kings of Judah and Israel and in Isaiah's vision.

l: priests, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: The priests, sons of Aaron, cleanse the temple's inner part and carry uncleanness to the court, then slaughter animals, sprinkle blood on the altar, and make the sin offering for all Israel amid trumpets. Too few to skin offerings, they are aided by Levites until sanctified.

l: temple cleansing, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: The temple cleansing was a sanctification of the LORD's house lasting eight days beyond its start and finishing on the sixteenth day of the first month. Priests cleansed the inner temple and brought uncleanness out; Levites carried it to the brook Kidron. Workers then reported to Hezekiah that the house, altar, table, and vessels, including Ahaz's discarded ones, were prepared.

l: sin offering, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: A sin offering of seven bulls, rams, lambs, and male goats for the kingdom, sanctuary, and Judah. Priests sprinkle the blood of bulls, rams, and lambs on the altar; the goats are presented to the king and assembly, who lay hands on them, then killed to atone for all Israel.

l: burnt offerings, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: brought_by_assembly_total seventy bulls, one hundred rams, two hundred lambs Hezekiah commands that the burnt offering be offered on the altar, and when it begins the LORD's song and the trumpets and David's instruments start and continue until it is finished. The assembly then brings seventy bulls, one hundred rams, and two hundred lambs as burnt offerings, along with consecrated things of six hundred cattle and three thousand sheep. The offerings are abundant, accompanied by fat of the peace offerings and drink offerings, and the Levites help skin them.

l: assembly (at Jerusalem), The Second Book of Chronicles
s: The assembly agreed with Hezekiah to keep the Passover in the second month, and a very great assembly gathered, removing the altars from Jerusalem. They kept the feast seven days, took counsel to keep seven more, received gifts of bulls and sheep from Hezekiah and the princes, and rejoiced greatly.

l: Passover, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Israel's Passover observance at Jerusalem under Hezekiah was delayed to the second month because too few priests were sanctified and people hadn't gathered. Killed on the fourteenth day, Levites served the unclean; irregular eating was forgiven after Hezekiah's prayer.

l: priests, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: The priests are a group descended from Aaron's sons who receive tithes and first fruits from Jerusalem's people so they can devote themselves to the law. Under Hezekiah they are organized into divisions for burnt and peace offerings, supplied by genealogy and named men, and have plenty left over. Under Josiah they are set in their offices, sprinkle Passover blood from the Levites, offer burnt offerings until night, and receive livestock from the rulers.

l: Levites, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: receives tithes and first fruits (offerings) [portion given by people of Jerusalem so they may devote themselves to the law] The Levites were appointed by divisions for service, thanksgiving and praise in the gates of the LORD's camp, and were supported by the people's portion. Conaniah, Shimei, Kore and the overseers under them were Levites who managed the stored offerings, and Levites twenty years old and upward were listed by genealogy for their offices.

l: Conaniah, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Conaniah, a Levite, is appointed ruler over the offerings, tithes and dedicated things stored in prepared rooms, with his brother Shimei second and ten overseers serving under him, appointed by Hezekiah and Azariah.

l: tithes and first fruits (offerings), The Second Book of Chronicles
s: After Hezekiah's command, the people gave first fruits of grain, new wine, oil, honey and all the field's increase, along with tithes of all things, cattle, sheep and dedicated things. These were brought in abundance and faithfully, and were stored and distributed to support the priests and Levites.

l: heaps (of offerings), The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Heaps of offerings (tithes, first fruits, cattle, sheep, dedicated things) were piled from the third to seventh month. Hezekiah, the princes and Azariah saw them, blessed the LORD, learned they were priestly surplus, and rooms were prepared in the LORD's house to store them.

l: Sennacherib, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Sennacherib, king of Assyria, invades Judah, attacks Lachish, and mocks Hezekiah and the LORD. After the LORD's angel destroys his mighty men and captains, he returns home in shame and is killed by his own sons in his god's house.

l: Babylon, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: sent ambassadors of the princes of Babylon [to inquire of the wonder in the land] Babylon receives Jehoiakim's captive party, vessels of the LORD's house, and Jehoiachin. All the vessels, treasures, and surviving people of Judah are brought there, where the survivors serve Nebuchadnezzar and his sons until Persia's reign.

l: Manasseh, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Manasseh was a king of Judah, son and successor of Hezekiah, who became king at twelve and reigned fifty-five years in Jerusalem. He first did great evil: rebuilding the high places, worshiping the army of the sky, building altars in the LORD's house, setting up an idol, making Asheroth, practicing sorcery, sacrificing his children by fire, and seducing Judah into worse evil than the nations. Assyrian captains took him in chains to Babylon, where he repented and learned the LORD was God. Restored, he built an outer wall, placed captains in fortified cities, removed foreign gods, rebuilt the LORD's altar, and commanded Judah to serve the LORD. He was buried in his own house; his son Amon succeeded him.

l: Assyrian siege of Jerusalem, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: has_outcome Assyrian forces cut off by angel; Sennacherib returned in shame [the LORD saved Jerusalem] Sennacherib's forces invade Judah and threaten Jerusalem while he attacks Lachish, and his servants taunt the people and deliver letters insulting the LORD. Hezekiah's preparations include stopping the springs and strengthening the wall. The threat ends when the LORD's angel destroys the Assyrian mighty men, leaders, and captains, and Sennacherib withdraws in shame.

l: Amon, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Amon, Manasseh's son, became king at twenty-two and reigned two years in Jerusalem. He did evil like his father, sacrificing to the engraved images Manasseh made, and never humbled himself, trespassing more and more. His servants conspired and killed him in his own house, and his son Josiah was made king.

l: Josiah, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Josiah was a king of Judah who became king at age eight and reigned thirty-one years in Jerusalem. He did what was right in the LORD's eyes and walked in the ways of David. He began seeking God in his eighth year, purged idolatry in his twelfth, and ordered the temple repaired in his eighteenth. Hearing the law, he tore his clothes and led a covenant renewal. Huldah promised him a peaceful death. He kept a great Passover, supplying thousands of animals from his own substance. Later he ignored Neco's warning from God, disguised himself, and was wounded by archers at Megiddo. He died in Jerusalem, was buried in his fathers' tombs, and was mourned by all Judah, Jerusalem, and Jeremiah.

l: high places, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: is_used_for sacrifice to the LORD [people still sacrificed there after reform] Manasseh rebuilt the high places that his father Hezekiah had broken down. Even after Manasseh's repentance and reforms, the people still sacrificed in the high places, but only to the LORD their God. The high places he built before humbling himself are recorded in the history of Hozai.

l: idol (Manasseh's engraved image), The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Manasseh made an engraved image of an idol and set it in God's house, the place where God had said He would put His name forever. After he humbled himself, he took the idol out of the LORD's house and cast it out of the city. Amon later sacrificed to the engraved images Manasseh had made.

l: altars, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Manasseh raised altars for the Baals and built altars for the army of the sky in the LORD's house and its two courts. After his restoration he removed all the altars he had built in the mountain of the LORD's house and in Jerusalem and cast them out of the city. He then rebuilt the LORD's altar and offered peace offerings and thanksgiving sacrifices on it.

l: Manasseh’s captivity and repentance, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Manasseh's captivity and repentance: because he and his people ignored the LORD, Assyrian captains bound him in chains and took him to Babylon. In distress he begged the LORD and humbled himself greatly. God heard him and restored him to Jerusalem and his kingdom; his prayer is recorded in the history of Hozai.

l: Shaphan, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Shaphan, scribe, son of Azaliah and father of Ahikam, is sent by Josiah to repair the LORD's house, receives and reads the found book to the king, and inquires of the LORD.

l: Hilkiah, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Hilkiah, high priest and ruler of God's house, received repair money, found the book of the LORD's law given by Moses, gave it to Shaphan, then at Josiah's command went with others to inquire of the LORD through Huldah.

l: Huldah, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Huldah, a prophetess in Jerusalem's second quarter, wife of Shallum, is consulted by Hilkiah and the king's men and declares coming judgment on the place but peace for Josiah in his lifetime.

l: book of the law, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: was_given_by Moses The book of the LORD's law given by Moses was found by Hilkiah in the LORD's house and passed to Shaphan, who read it to Josiah. Its words caused the king to tear his clothes and seek the LORD's word. Josiah later read it as the book of the covenant to all the people.

l: idolatrous objects and altars, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: The altars of the Baals, incense altars, Asherah poles, engraved images, and molten images were broken down, cut down, and ground to dust under Josiah's direction. The dust was scattered on the graves of those who had sacrificed to them. This extended throughout Israel, and Josiah took away all abominations from the lands of the children of Israel.

l: temple repair, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: repairs house of the LORD In his eighteenth year Josiah sent Shaphan, Maaseiah, and Joah to repair the house of the LORD with money delivered through Hilkiah to the overseers and workmen. The men worked faithfully under Levite overseers Jahath, Obadiah, Zechariah, and Meshullam. During this work the book of the law was found.

l: purge of idolatry, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Josiah's purge of idolatry began in his twelfth year: he removed high places and images from Judah and Jerusalem, burned priests' bones on their altars, extended it to Manasseh, Ephraim, Simeon, Naphtali, returned to Jerusalem, before temple repair.

l: covenant renewal, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: A covenant renewal at the LORD's house: Josiah gathers the elders and all people, reads them the covenant book, pledges wholehearted obedience to the LORD's commandments, and has those in Jerusalem and Benjamin stand and act according to it.

l: Passover (Josiah's Passover), The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Josiah's Passover was a Passover kept to the LORD in Jerusalem on the fourteenth day of the first month, in the eighteenth year of his reign. The king, princes, and Levite chiefs supplied the animals, and service followed the king's commandment. Unequalled since Samuel, it was followed by seven days of unleavened bread.

l: king of Egypt (Neco), The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Neco, king of Egypt, marches against Carchemish by the Euphrates, sends envoys telling Josiah God commanded his haste and warning him not to oppose God; Josiah refuses to turn back and fights him at Megiddo.

l: Jeremiah, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: is_a prophet [spoke from the LORD's mouth] Jeremiah the prophet speaks from the LORD's mouth, but Zedekiah does not humble himself before him. His word is fulfilled in the seventy years of the land's Sabbath desolation, and again when the LORD stirs up Cyrus.

l: battle at Megiddo (Josiah's death), The Second Book of Chronicles
s: The battle at Megiddo pits Josiah against Neco in the valley of Megiddo. Disguised, Josiah is shot by archers, moved to a second chariot, and taken to Jerusalem, where he dies and is buried. All Judah mourns; Jeremiah and singers lament, becoming an Israelite ordinance.

l: Jehoiakim, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Jehoiakim, formerly Eliakim, was renamed and installed as king of Judah by Egypt's king in place of his brother Joahaz. He reigned eleven years in Jerusalem from age twenty-five, did evil in the LORD's sight, was fettered by Nebuchadnezzar, and was succeeded by his son Jehoiachin.

l: Nebuchadnezzar, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, attacks Jehoiakim, takes the LORD's house vessels to his Babylon temple, brings Jehoiachin to Babylon, and installs Zedekiah as king, who later rebels despite his oath.

l: chiefs of the priests and the people, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Priestly and popular leaders grievously trespass, imitating the nations' abominations and defiling the LORD's temple, then mock his messengers and prophets until his wrath becomes beyond remedy.

l: destruction of Jerusalem, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: The Chaldean king's conquest of Jerusalem: he kills young and old even in the sanctuary, plunders vessels and treasures, burns God's house and palaces, breaks the wall, exiles survivors to Babylon, leaving the land desolate seventy years.

l: Cyrus, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: Cyrus, king of Persia, is commanded by the LORD to build a house in Jerusalem; in his first year, his spirit stirred, he proclaims throughout his kingdom that the LORD gave him all earth's kingdoms.

l: proclamation of Cyrus, The Second Book of Chronicles
s: is_issued_by Cyrus [throughout his kingdom, also in writing] The proclamation is made orally and in writing throughout Cyrus's kingdom. It states that the LORD, the God of heaven, commanded Cyrus to build him a house in Jerusalem in Judah, and invites any of his people to go up, with the LORD's presence.

l: The Book of Haggai
s: This is the book of Haggai, a short prophetic text set in the second year of King Darius, in which the LORD of Armies speaks through the prophet Haggai to Zerubbabel the governor of Judah, Joshua the high priest, and the remnant of the people. In chapter 1, the LORD rebukes them for living in paneled houses while his house lies waste, ties their poor harvests to that neglect, and commands them to build. The leaders and people obey, the LORD affirms he is with them, and work begins on the twenty-fourth day of the sixth month. Chapter 2 gives three further messages. The people are told to be strong because the house's latter glory will exceed the former. Haggai uses the priests' answers on holiness and uncleanness to show the people's unclean state, and the LORD promises blessing from that day. Finally, he promises to shake the heavens and earth, overthrow kingdoms, and make Zerubbabel his signet ring.

l: the LORD of Armies, The Book of Haggai
s: The LORD of Armies is God of the remnant of the people, speaking through the messenger Haggai. He first rebukes them for neglecting his ruined house while living in paneled houses, explains their poor harvests, and commands them to build, stirring leaders and remnant to begin. He then encourages them, being present as they work, promising glory in the house, peace, blessing, ownership of silver and gold, overthrow of chariots and riders, and Zerubbabel as his chosen signet ring.

l: Haggai, The Book of Haggai
s: Haggai is a prophet and the LORD's messenger. He delivers the LORD's word to Zerubbabel, Joshua, and the remnant, telling them 'I am with you,' and the people obey. Later, on specified dates, he delivers further messages and questions the priests about holiness and uncleanness, declaring the people and their offerings unclean.

l: Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, The Book of Haggai
s: Zerubbabel, son of Shealtiel, is governor of Judah and the LORD of Armies' servant. Addressed through Haggai, he obeys with Joshua and the remnant, and the LORD stirs his spirit to work on the LORD's house. He is told to be strong, and promised that when kingdoms fall he will be made like a signet ring, chosen.

l: Joshua the son of Jehozadak, The Book of Haggai
s: Joshua, son of Jehozadak, is the high priest addressed with Zerubbabel through Haggai. He obeys the LORD, his spirit is stirred to join the house work, and he is told to be strong because the LORD is with him.

l: the temple (the LORD’s house), The Book of Haggai
s: The LORD of Armies' house lies waste while the people live in paneled houses and say the time has not come. The LORD commands them to bring wood and build it, for his pleasure and glory. Work begins in Darius's second year; it is promised greater latter glory than the former.

l: remnant of the people, The Book of Haggai
s: The remnant of the people, with Zerubbabel and Joshua, obeys the LORD and Haggai's words, fears Him, and, with stirred spirits, works on the LORD's house. They are then told to be strong and unafraid, described as unclean with their work, reminded of failed harvests without repentance, and promised blessing from that day.

l: the shaking of heavens and earth, The Book of Haggai
s: A promised shaking of heavens, earth, sea, dry land and all nations by the LORD of Armies. Soon after, nations' treasure comes to the house; he then promises Zerubbabel to overthrow thrones, destroy nations' strength, and make chariots and horsemen fall by one another's swords.

l: The Book of Zechariah
s: This document is the book of the prophet Zechariah, son of Berechiah and son of Iddo, a series of visions and oracles dated to the reign of Darius. It centers on the LORD (the LORD of Armies), his jealous love for Jerusalem and Zion, and the restoration of his people and temple. Key figures are Zechariah, the interpreting angel, Joshua the high priest, Zerubbabel, and the promised Branch and humble King. Chapters 1-6 present night visions. After a call to return to the LORD, Zechariah sees horsemen among myrtle trees, and the LORD answers with mercy for Jerusalem after seventy years. Further visions follow: horns and craftsmen, a man measuring Jerusalem, Joshua's filthy garments replaced with clean clothing, a golden lamp stand with two olive trees and the word 'Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit' to Zerubbabel, a flying scroll of curse, a woman called Wickedness carried to Shinar, and four chariots going through the earth. Crowns are made for Joshua, with the Branch promised to build the temple and rule as priest. Chapters 7-8 turn to a question from Bethel about continued fasting. The LORD challenges their motives, recalls the former prophets' demands for justice and compassion, and recounts how the ancestors' hardness led to scattering. He then promises to dwell in Jerusalem, the City of Truth, turning fasts into joyful feasts, and nations will seek him. Chapters 9-14 are oracles. Judgment falls on neighboring cities, while Zion's righteous, lowly King comes on a donkey, speaking peace to nations. The LORD promises to restore Judah and Ephraim and condemns false shepherds. The narrator then acts as a shepherd with two staffs, Favor and Union, is paid thirty pieces of silver thrown to the potter, and breaks both staffs, and a worthless shepherd is announced. Jerusalem is to be besieged, yet the LORD defends it; a spirit of grace is poured out, and the people mourn for one they pierced. A fountain cleanses sin, idols and false prophets are removed, and a refined remnant calls on his name. The book ends with a final day when nations attack Jerusalem, the LORD stands on the split Mount of Olives, becomes King over all the earth, living waters flow, survivors keep the feast of booths, and everything becomes holy to the LORD.

l: LORD of Armies, The Book of Zechariah
s: LORD of Armies is the divine title and speaking figure throughout these records, presented as God of the returning remnant of Israel and as King over all the earth. He begins by calling the people to return, recalling his great displeasure with their fathers, and declaring great jealousy for Jerusalem and Zion and anger at the nations at ease who added to the calamity. He promises to be a wall of fire around Jerusalem and glory in her middle, to dwell within Zion, to inherit Judah, and to choose Jerusalem again, having roused himself from his holy habitation. He rebukes Satan, sets a stone with seven eyes before Joshua, and promises to bring out his servant the Branch, who will build the temple. He declares the work will be done not by might but by his Spirit, and sends out a curse into the houses of the thief and the false swearer. He sends his word to Zechariah, questioning the people's fasting and recalling that, because they refused to listen, he scattered them in a whirlwind. He then reverses course: he plans good for Jerusalem and Judah, saves his people from east and west to be their God in truth and righteousness, hates false oaths, and commands truth and peace. He judges neighboring cities, encamps around his house, and saves his people as a flock, and his goodness and beauty are called great. He gives rain, is angry at the shepherds, visits his flock, strengthens Judah, and has mercy on the house of Joseph. He also declares no more pity for the inhabitants of the land and strikes a worthless shepherd. As creator who stretches out the heavens, lays the earth's foundation, and forms the spirit of man, he makes Jerusalem a burdensome stone, saves Judah's tents first, and pours out a spirit of grace. In that day he opens a fountain for sin, cuts off idols, removes prophets and the spirit of impurity, strikes the shepherd, refines a remaining third, and calls them his people. The records end with him gathering the nations against Jerusalem, fighting them and standing on the Mount of Olives, becoming King over all the earth with one name, and being worshiped as the LORD of Armies, withholding rain from those who skip the feast of booths.

l: Zechariah, The Book of Zechariah
s: Zechariah is a prophet, son of Berechiah and grandson of Iddo, who receives the LORD's word. In the first chapter he is given the word in Darius's second year and sees night visions of horses, four horns and four craftsmen, asking the angel to explain them. Later he sees a flying scroll and an ephah basket carried by winged women. In Darius's fourth year he relays the LORD's rebuke to the people and priests, commanding true judgment and kindness.

l: fathers (Zechariah's audience's fathers), The Book of Zechariah
s: disobeyed former prophets [did not hear or listen] The fathers were the object of the LORD's great displeasure, and they did not hear or listen when the former prophets urged them to turn from evil ways. The LORD's words and decrees overtook them, and they then repented, saying the LORD had dealt with them according to their ways and practices.

l: man on the red horse (in Zechariah's vision), The Book of Zechariah
s: location among the myrtle trees [in a ravine] The man on a red horse stands among the myrtle trees in a ravine, with red, brown, and white horses behind him. He explains that the horses are those the LORD has sent to go back and forth through the earth.

l: angel who talked with me (Zechariah's interpreting angel), The Book of Zechariah
s: The angel who talks with Zechariah is the interpreter of his visions. In Chapter 1 he promises to show what the horses are, receives kind and comforting words from the LORD, tells Zechariah to proclaim the LORD's jealousy for Jerusalem and Zion, and explains the four horns and craftsmen. In Chapter 2 he goes out and is met by another angel, who sends word about Jerusalem. In Chapter 5 he explains the ephah basket, names the woman Wickedness, confines her under the lead weight, and says the basket goes to Shinar. In Chapter 6 he explains the chariots as the four winds.

l: the LORD's angel, The Book of Zechariah
s: The LORD's angel stands among the myrtle trees and receives the report that all the earth is at rest and in peace. He then asks the LORD of Armies how long he will withhold mercy from Jerusalem and the cities of Judah after seventy years of indignation. The LORD's angel presides over the scene in which Joshua stands before him, and stands by as Joshua is given a clean turban and clothed. He solemnly assures Joshua and delivers the LORD of Armies' conditional promise.

l: horses (in the vision), The Book of Zechariah
s: Red, brown, and white horses stand behind the man among the myrtle trees; sent by the LORD to roam the earth, they report all the earth is at rest and in peace.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Zechariah
s: Jerusalem is a city whose fortunes the records trace from judgment through trial to restoration. It begins under the LORD's indignation for seventy years, with the LORD's angel pleading for mercy. The LORD then declares his jealousy for it, his return with mercy, and that he will again choose it and have his house built there. A man with a measuring line is sent to measure it, and it is told it will be inhabited as villages without walls because of its multitude of men and livestock, with the LORD as a wall of fire around it and glory in its midst. It will be called The City of Truth, with old men and women and playing boys and girls filling its streets, and many peoples coming to seek the LORD. Its King comes, and the horse is cut off from it. Yet it also becomes a cup of reeling and a burdensome stone for surrounding peoples, as all nations gather against it and Judah shares the siege. The LORD defends its inhabitants, the feeble become like David, and it dwells again in its own place amid great mourning. In the end it is taken, its houses rifled, and half its people go into captivity. Afterward living waters flow from it, it is lifted up and dwells safely with no more curse, nations come to worship, and every pot is holy to the LORD of Armies.

l: Zion, The Book of Zechariah
s: Zion is a place and people, also called the daughter of Zion, that the LORD cherishes as the apple of his eye. The records open with his great jealousy and a promise of comfort. Zion is then told to flee Babylon's daughter and rejoice as he comes to dwell within her. He declares he has returned, despite wrath. Finally her King comes, and her sons are made like a mighty man's sword against Greece.

l: Judah, The Book of Zechariah
s: Judah is both a people and a land, the house of Judah and its cities, whose fortunes the LORD reverses across the records. It begins under the LORD's indignation for seventy years and scattered by the horns of the nations, once a curse among the nations. It is then promised salvation and a role as a blessing: the LORD plans good for it, and its fasts become joy, gladness, and cheerful feasts. It is the LORD's bow, loaded with Ephraim, and his flock, made like a majestic horse in battle, from which come the cornerstone, tent peg, battle bow and every ruler. Its sons are stirred up against the sons of Greece. In the siege of Jerusalem the LORD opens his eyes on Judah and saves its tents first. It ends fighting at Jerusalem, gathering the nations' wealth, with every pot in Judah holy to the LORD of Armies.

l: nations, The Book of Zechariah
s: The nations are at ease, and the LORD is very angry with them because he was only a little displeased but they added to the calamity. The horns of the nations that lifted up their horn against Judah are to be cast down.

l: four horns (in the vision), The Book of Zechariah
s: scattered Judah [also Israel and Jerusalem] Zechariah sees four horns, which the angel says have scattered Judah, Israel, and Jerusalem. They represent the horns of the nations that lifted up their horn against the land of Judah to scatter it.

l: four craftsmen (in the vision), The Book of Zechariah
s: purpose cast down the horns of the nations [terrify the horns] The LORD shows Zechariah four craftsmen. They have come to terrify the horns and cast down the horns of the nations that scattered Judah.

l: man with a measuring line, The Book of Zechariah
s: A man holding a measuring line appears to the narrator in Chapter 2 and, when asked, says he is going to measure Jerusalem's width and length.

l: narrator (Zechariah), The Book of Zechariah
s: The narrator lifts up his eyes and sees four chariots come out from between two bronze mountains, and asks the angel what they are. He then receives the LORD's word instructing him to take silver and gold from the exiles, make crowns, set them on Joshua's head, and deliver the message about the Branch.

l: many nations, The Book of Zechariah
s: will_join the LORD [in that day; will be his people] Many nations are said to join themselves to the LORD in that day and to become his people. A separate group of nations that plundered the LORD's people will themselves become plunder to those who served them, when the LORD shakes his hand over them.

l: people of Jerusalem (Jerusalem's inhabitants), The Book of Zechariah
s: The inhabitants of Jerusalem, men and livestock, are numerous enough that the city will be inhabited as villages without walls. They are protected by the LORD as a wall of fire. Those in the north and with Babylon are called to flee and come, having been spread abroad like the four winds of the sky.

l: Joshua the son of Jehozadak, The Book of Zechariah
s: Joshua is a high priest who first appears standing before the LORD's angel in filthy garments, opposed by Satan yet called a burning stick plucked from the fire. His garments are replaced with rich clothing and a clean turban, and he is promised authority to judge and keep the LORD's house if he walks in the LORD's ways. He and his fellows are a sign. Later, crowns of silver and gold from the exiles Heldai, Tobijah, and Jedaiah are to be set on his head, with a message about the Branch.

l: Satan, The Book of Zechariah
s: is_adversary_of Joshua the high priest [stands at his right hand] Satan stands at Joshua's right hand to be his adversary. The LORD rebukes him twice, and he is not recorded as saying anything.

l: filthy garments (Joshua's garments), The Book of Zechariah
s: Joshua is clothed in filthy garments as he stands before the angel. Those standing before the speaker are told to take them off him, and he is clothed with rich clothing instead.

l: Joshua's iniquity, The Book of Zechariah
s: is_removed_from Joshua the high priest [caused to pass by the LORD] The speaker declares that he has caused Joshua's iniquity to pass from him, which is paired with the removal of the filthy garments. The LORD also says he will remove the iniquity of that land in one day.

l: the Branch, The Book of Zechariah
s: The Branch is the LORD's servant, promised in Chapter 3 with Joshua and his fellows as a sign. In Chapter 6 he grows up from his place, builds the LORD's temple, bears glory, and sits and rules on his throne as priest, with peace counseled between both roles.

l: Zerubbabel, The Book of Zechariah
s: Zerubbabel is a person who laid the house's foundation and is promised to finish it. Told the work depends on the Spirit, not might, he will see the mountain become a plain, hold the plumb line, and bring out the capstone with shouts of 'Grace, grace.'

l: flying scroll, The Book of Zechariah
s: A flying scroll, twenty by ten cubits, seen by the narrator in Chapter 5 and identified as the curse going out over the whole land.

l: curse (the flying scroll's curse), The Book of Zechariah
s: The curse goes out over the whole land, cutting off thieves according to one side and false swearers according to the other. The LORD says it will enter the houses of the thief and of the one who swears falsely by his name, and remain there until it destroys the house with its timber and stones.

l: ephah basket, The Book of Zechariah
s: An ephah basket depicted as the appearance of them throughout the land, topped with a talent-weight lead cover and holding a woman called Wickedness. She is thrown in, it is sealed, and two women lift it skyward to Shinar.

l: Wickedness, The Book of Zechariah
s: Wickedness is a woman sitting in an ephah basket; an angel names her, forces her down, seals the basket with lead, and she is carried to Shinar, to be set in her own house.

l: two women (who carry the ephah basket), The Book of Zechariah
s: Two women appear with the wind in their wings, which are like the wings of a stork. They lift up the ephah basket between earth and sky to carry it away.

l: Shinar, The Book of Zechariah
s: Shinar is named as the destination of the ephah basket. A house is to be built there for Wickedness, and when it is prepared she will be set in her own place.

l: four chariots, The Book of Zechariah
s: Four powerful chariots drawn by red, black, white, and dappled horses emerge from between two bronze mountains, are identified as the four winds of the sky, and go out to the north and south countries, roaming the earth.

l: four winds of the sky, The Book of Zechariah
s: stands_before LORD [Lord of all the earth] The four chariots are identified as the four winds of the sky, which go out from standing before the Lord of all the earth. They are told to go around and through the earth and do so, and those going toward the north country are said to have quieted the LORD's spirit in the north.

l: crowns, The Book of Zechariah
s: Crowns made of silver and gold taken from Babylonian exiles are first set on the head of Joshua the high priest, then afterwards belong to Helem, Tobijah, Jedaiah, and Hen son of Zephaniah as a memorial in the LORD's temple.

l: people of Bethel, The Book of Zechariah
s: The people of Bethel, a group, send Sharezer, Regem Melech and their men to entreat the LORD's favor and ask whether to keep weeping in the fifth month, prompting the LORD's longer response on fasting and obedience.

l: fast in the fifth month, The Book of Zechariah
s: A fifth-month fast with weeping, kept seventy years alongside the seventh month's; the LORD questions whether the people truly fasted to him, since they ate and drank only for themselves.

l: people of the land, The Book of Zechariah
s: The people of the land, together with the priests, are the ones Zechariah is told to address. They are questioned about whether their fasts of seventy years in the fifth and seventh months were really made to the LORD.

l: ancestors who refused to listen (they), The Book of Zechariah
s: Ancestors who refused to listen turned their backs, stopped their ears and hardened their hearts like flint, rejecting the law and the prophets' words. Consequently, great wrath of the LORD fell on them, He ignored their calls, and a whirlwind scattered them among unknown nations.

l: commands of justice and kindness, The Book of Zechariah
s: Commands of justice and kindness, proclaimed by former prophets, require true judgment and compassion, forbid oppressing widows, the fatherless, foreigners and the poor, and forbid devising evil against a brother, recalled from Jerusalem's prosperous days.

l: wrath of the LORD, The Book of Zechariah
s: is_characterized_as great Great wrath comes from the LORD of Armies because the people hardened their hearts and refused to hear the law and the words sent by his Spirit through the former prophets. It results in the LORD refusing to listen to their calls and scattering them among the nations.

l: pleasant land, The Book of Zechariah
s: has_state desolate [no one passed through or returned] The pleasant land is left desolate after the people are scattered, so that no one passes through or returns. The text says the people themselves made it desolate.

l: remnant of this people, The Book of Zechariah
s: inherits peace, fruit, increase and dew [granted by the LORD of Armies] The remnant is told that its present marvel is not too marvelous for the LORD, and that he will no longer treat it as in the former days of no wages, no peace, and strife with neighbors. It will inherit peaceful seed, fruitful vine, productive ground, and dew from heaven.

l: many peoples and strong nations, The Book of Zechariah
s: seek LORD of Armies [in Jerusalem] Many peoples, inhabitants of many cities, and strong nations are foretold to come to Jerusalem to entreat the favor of the LORD and seek the LORD of Armies, urging one another to go speedily. Ten men from all the languages of the nations will take hold of a Jew's skirt, saying they will go with him because they have heard God is with them.

l: truth and peace, The Book of Zechariah
s: Truth and peace are what the people are commanded to practice: speaking truth to neighbors and executing the judgment of truth and peace in the gates. The people are told to love truth and peace, in connection with the fasts becoming joyful feasts.

l: Tyre, The Book of Zechariah
s: Tyre is a very wise place bordering Hamath, with a self-built stronghold and abundant silver and gold; it is condemned, its sea power to be struck, dispossessed by the Lord and devoured by fire.

l: Philistines, The Book of Zechariah
s: has_attribute pride [the LORD will cut it off] The Philistine cities Ashkelon, Gaza, Ekron and Ashdod will see Tyre's fate and fear, with Gaza writhing and losing its king and Ashkelon left uninhabited. Foreigners will dwell in Ashdod, and the LORD will cut off Philistine pride, take blood and abominations from their mouths, and leave a remnant for God, like a chieftain in Judah, with Ekron as a Jebusite.

l: king (the coming King of Zion), The Book of Zechariah
s: The coming King of Zion is portrayed as righteous, lowly, and bearing salvation, arriving riding a donkey's colt. He then speaks peace to the nations, and his dominion extends from sea to sea and from the River to the earth's ends.

l: Ephraim, The Book of Zechariah
s: is_like mighty man [future state; heart rejoices as through wine] Ephraim will be like a mighty man, and their heart will rejoice as with wine. Their children will see it and rejoice, being glad in the LORD.

l: prisoners of hope, The Book of Zechariah
s: Prisoners of hope are captives freed by the LORD from the waterless pit because of the covenant's blood; they are told to turn to the stronghold and promised double restoration.

l: Judah's people (the LORD's people), The Book of Zechariah
s: Judah's people, the LORD's people, are defended by the LORD of Armies. They overcome enemies with sling stones, drink and roar as with wine, and are saved as a flock. They finally shine like crown jewels lifted over his land, flourishing with grain and new wine.

l: house of Joseph, The Book of Zechariah
s: The LORD says he will save the house of Joseph and bring them back out of mercy. They will be as though he had not cast them off.

l: Assyria, The Book of Zechariah
s: has pride [will be brought down] Assyria is a land from which the LORD will gather his people. Its pride will be brought down.

l: Egypt, The Book of Zechariah
s: Egypt is a land and nation from which the LORD will bring his people back. First, its scepter will depart and the Nile's depths will dry up. Later, it is an example among the earth's families: if it doesn't go up to Jerusalem for the feast of booths, no rain will fall.

l: shepherds, The Book of Zechariah
s: is_lacking shepherd [people are oppressed because there is no shepherd] The shepherds draw the LORD's kindled anger, and he says he will punish the male goats. The people go like oppressed sheep because there is no shepherd.

l: people of Israel (returning exiles), The Book of Zechariah
s: The returning exiles are a people promised redemption: the LORD will gather them from Egypt and Assyria, where they were sown among peoples and remember him. They will return with their children, increase as before, fill Gilead and Lebanon beyond capacity, and walk in his name.

l: narrator (the shepherd speaking), The Book of Zechariah
s: The narrator is a shepherd who speaks for the LORD. He feeds the oppressed flock destined for slaughter, takes staffs Favor and Union, and cuts off three shepherds in a month. He then quits, breaks both staffs, receives thirty silver pieces, throws them to the potter at the LORD's command, and is told to take a foolish shepherd's equipment.

l: shepherds (of the flock), The Book of Zechariah
s: disposition_toward_flock no pity The shepherds wail because their glory is destroyed, and they show no pity to the flock. The narrator cuts off three shepherds in one month because his soul was weary of them and their soul loathed him.

l: flock of slaughter, The Book of Zechariah
s: is_treated_by_buyers buyers and sellers of the flock [buyers slaughter them without punishment] The flock is slaughtered by buyers who go unpunished and sold by sellers who thank the LORD for their riches, while its own shepherds don't pity it. The narrator feeds it, especially the oppressed, then declines to feed it further and lets the dying die and the survivors eat each other's flesh. The poor of the flock who listened to him recognize the broken staff as the LORD's word.

l: inhabitants of the land, The Book of Zechariah
s: The LORD says He will no longer pity the inhabitants of the land. He will deliver each man into the hand of his neighbor and of his king, and they will strike the land without deliverance from Him.

l: Favor, The Book of Zechariah
s: Favor is a staff the shepherd narrator takes as one of two, symbolizing his covenant with all peoples; he cuts it apart, breaking the covenant, and the poor of the flock recognize it as the LORD's word.

l: Union, The Book of Zechariah
s: Union is the narrator-shepherd's second staff, symbolizing brotherhood between Judah and Israel; in Chapter 11 he takes it, then cuts it apart, breaking that brotherhood.

l: thirty pieces of silver, The Book of Zechariah
s: Thirty pieces of silver are the narrator's wages, an ironic handsome valuation of him, weighed out and then, at the LORD's command, thrown to the potter in the LORD's house.

l: foolish shepherd, The Book of Zechariah
s: The foolish shepherd is a worthless shepherd the LORD raises up in the land. He neglects the flock, neither visiting, seeking, healing nor feeding it, while eating the fat sheep and tearing their hoofs. Woe is pronounced on him: judgment comes as a withered arm and blinded right eye.

l: chieftains of Judah, The Book of Zechariah
s: The chieftains of Judah resolve inwardly that Jerusalem's inhabitants are their strength through the LORD of Armies, their God. They are then portrayed as a fiery pan among wood, devouring surrounding peoples on every side.

l: nations (the peoples surrounding Jerusalem), The Book of Zechariah
s: The surrounding peoples will drink from the cup of reeling that Jerusalem becomes, and all the nations of the earth will be gathered against it. Those who burden themselves with the stone will be severely wounded, their horses will be struck with blindness, and the LORD will seek to destroy them. The chieftains of Judah will devour the surrounding peoples.

l: house of David, The Book of Zechariah
s: The house of David is a royal family group that the LORD elevates to be like God, like the LORD's angel, and pours with a spirit of grace and supplication. Its glory is not magnified above Judah, and it mourns apart with the house of Nathan.

l: the pierced one, The Book of Zechariah
s: The pierced one is a figure the LORD says people have pierced; they will look to him, then mourn bitterly for him as for an only son and firstborn.

l: mourning in Jerusalem, The Book of Zechariah
s: A great mourning foretold for that day, likened to the mourning of Hadadrimmon in the valley of Megiddo; the whole land mourns, each family apart and wives apart, including the houses of David, Nathan, Levi, Shimeites and all remaining families.

l: fountain (opened to David's house), The Book of Zechariah
s: A fountain to be opened in that day to David's house and Jerusalem's inhabitants, its purpose being cleansing from sin and uncleanness.

l: prophets, The Book of Zechariah
s: The prophets are a group who, in that day, will be removed from the land with the spirit of impurity. Any who still prophesy are condemned by their own parents and stabbed. Ashamed of their visions, they drop the hairy mantle, deny being prophets, claim to be farmers, and explain their wounds as received in friends' houses.

l: shepherd (the LORD's shepherd), The Book of Zechariah
s: The LORD's shepherd, described as the man close to the LORD of Armies, is targeted when the LORD calls the sword to awake against him and commands he be struck, scattering the sheep.

l: land, The Book of Zechariah
s: A land to be purged of idol names, prophets and the spirit of impurity; two parts of it will be cut off and die, while the remaining third part is left in it.

l: people of the land (the refined third), The Book of Zechariah
s: The remnant third of the land's people is refined by fire like silver. They call on the LORD of Armies, who hears them, declares them his people, and they answer that the LORD is their God.

l: refining by fire, The Book of Zechariah
s: is_compared_to refining of silver and testing of gold The LORD will bring the surviving third into the fire, refining them as silver is refined and testing them as gold is tested. The outcome is that they call on his name, he hears them, and they are affirmed as his people.

l: nations, The Book of Zechariah
s: All nations are gathered against Jerusalem to battle and take the city. The LORD fights them, and their peoples are struck by a plague and panic, and their wealth is gathered by Judah. Survivors must go up year to year to worship the King and keep the feast of booths, or no rain falls on them.

l: Mount of Olives, The Book of Zechariah
s: The Mount of Olives lies east of Jerusalem and is where the LORD's feet stand in that day; it splits east to west, half north, half south, forming a great valley for people's escape.

l: plague on the peoples, The Book of Zechariah
s: A plague sent by the LORD on the peoples who fought against Jerusalem: their flesh, eyes and tongues rot away as they stand, panic makes them turn on each other, and the same plague strikes their animals.

l: feast of booths, The Book of Zechariah
s: is_attended_by nations [survivors go up yearly to worship the King] The survivors of the nations that came against Jerusalem are to go up yearly to worship the King, the LORD of Armies, and keep the feast of booths. Nations that do not go up receive no rain, which is called the plague and punishment for failing to keep it.

l: day of the LORD, The Book of Zechariah
s: has_character unique day, not day and not night [light at evening time] The day of the LORD is announced as a day when plunder is divided within Jerusalem, and as a unique day known to the LORD, neither day nor night, with light at evening time. On it there is no light, cold or frost, living waters flow from Jerusalem, and the LORD is King over all the earth. It also brings the final battle, the plague on the nations, and the holiness of all things in Jerusalem and Judah.

l: The Book of Malachi
s: This document is the Book of Malachi, four chapters of prophetic speech in which the LORD of Armies addresses Israel through Malachi, rebuking the people and especially the priests for unfaithfulness while promising purification, judgment, and blessing. In chapter 1 the LORD affirms his love for Israel by contrasting Jacob with Esau, whose land Edom he has made desolate and will keep from rebuilding. He then accuses the priests of despising his name by offering polluted bread and blind, lame, or sick animals, gifts they would never give their governor, and he declares that his name is great among the nations and curses the deceiver who sacrifices a defective animal. Chapter 2 warns the priests of a curse, contrasting them with Levi, who revered the LORD, taught true law, and turned many from iniquity, whereas they have caused many to stumble and corrupted the covenant. It then charges Judah with treachery, including marrying the daughter of a foreign god, with faithlessness to the wife of one's youth and with divorce, and with wearying the LORD by calling evildoers good. Chapter 3 announces a messenger who will prepare the way before the Lord's sudden coming to his temple, like a refiner's fire and launderers' soap, purifying the sons of Levi and bringing swift judgment on sorcerers, adulterers, perjurers, and oppressors of workers, widows, orphans, and foreigners. Because the LORD does not change, Jacob's sons are not consumed; he calls them to return, accuses them of robbing him in tithes and offerings, and invites them to bring the whole tithe and test him for overflowing blessing. Against the complaint that serving God is vain, those who feared the LORD are recorded in a book of memory and will be spared as his own possession. Chapter 4 describes the coming day burning like a furnace over the proud and wicked, while for those who fear his name the sun of righteousness rises with healing. The people are told to remember the law of Moses, and the LORD promises to send Elijah before the great and terrible day to turn the hearts of fathers and children, lest he strike the earth with a curse.

l: LORD of Armies, The Book of Malachi
s: LORD of Armies is the divine speaker throughout the records, presented as a great King whose name is great among the nations. He declares love for Jacob and hatred for Esau, and shows lasting wrath toward Edom. He is called father and master, and creator of the people. In the opening chapters he rebukes the priests, takes no pleasure in them, rejects defective offerings, and recalls his covenant with Levi. He is witness between a man and the wife of his youth, and is wearied by people who call evildoers good. Later he announces a messenger to prepare his way, and says he will come suddenly like a refiner's fire to purify the sons of Levi. He is a swift witness against wrongdoers, declares himself unchanging, and spares those who fear him as a man spares his son. The records close with the command to remember the law of Moses his servant, given at Horeb, and the promise to send Elijah before the great day of the LORD, so that he need not strike the earth with a curse.

l: Israel, The Book of Malachi
s: Israel is addressed by the LORD through Malachi and told that he has loved them, though they ask how. They are told they will see the LORD's treatment of Edom and say that the LORD is great even beyond the border of Israel.

l: Jacob, The Book of Malachi
s: Jacob is named as Esau's brother and as the one the LORD loved. His case is the LORD's answer to Israel's question about how he has loved them.

l: Esau, The Book of Malachi
s: is_brother_of Jacob Esau is identified as Jacob's brother, yet the LORD says he hated him. The LORD made Esau's mountains a desolation and gave his heritage to the jackals of the wilderness.

l: Edom, The Book of Malachi
s: is_called The Wicked Land [by men, after the LORD throws down what they build] Edom says it has been beaten down but will return and build the waste places. The LORD of Armies replies that they may build but he will throw down, and they will be called 'The Wicked Land,' the people against whom the LORD shows wrath forever.

l: priests (the LORD's priests addressed), The Book of Malachi
s: The priests are the LORD's addressed messengers, whose lips should keep knowledge. In chapter 1 they are accused of despising his name by offering polluted bread and blind, lame, sick, or violently taken animals, and he refuses their offerings. In chapter 2 he warns of a curse on them and their blessings, rebuke of their offspring, and dung on their faces. They turned from the path, caused many to stumble, corrupted the covenant of Levi, and showed partiality in the law, so he made them contemptible and wicked before the people.

l: sacrifices (defective offerings), The Book of Malachi
s: Offerings of blind, lame, and sick animals are called evil, and the LORD asks whether a governor would accept such gifts. He rejects them, contrasting them with the pure offering made to his name among the nations. He curses the deceiver who vows a male from his flock but sacrifices a defective thing.

l: Levi, The Book of Malachi
s: Levi is depicted as an ideal priest who held a covenant of life and peace with the LORD, revered and stood in awe of his name, spoke truth without unrighteousness, walked with the LORD in peace and uprightness, turned many from iniquity, and models a priest whose lips keep knowledge.

l: covenant of Levi, The Book of Malachi
s: is_corrupted_by priests The covenant of Levi is the LORD's covenant of life and peace given to Levi so that he would be reverent. The priests are accused of having corrupted it by turning from the path and causing many to stumble in the law. The commandment is sent so that this covenant may be with Levi.

l: Judah, The Book of Malachi
s: Judah is portrayed as treacherous: it committed abomination in Israel and Jerusalem, profaning the LORD's holiness by marrying a foreign god's daughter. The record ends with the LORD vowing to cut off the offender from Jacob's tents, despite offerings.

l: wife of your youth, The Book of Malachi
s: is_role_of companion [wife of your covenant] The wife of your youth is described as a man's companion and the wife of his covenant, against whom men have dealt treacherously. The LORD has been witness between them and her husband. The people are told to take heed to their spirit and not deal treacherously against her, since hating and divorcing covers a man's garment with violence.

l: Israelite nation (the addressed people), The Book of Malachi
s: The people, called the sons of Jacob, are not consumed because the LORD does not change, though they have turned from his ordinances since the days of their fathers. They are told to return to him, are accused of robbing him in tithes and offerings and are called cursed, and are promised blessing if they bring the whole tithe. They are also rebuked for saying that serving God is vain and that the proud and wicked prosper, and they are told they will again discern between the righteous and the wicked.

l: messenger (the messenger who prepares the way), The Book of Malachi
s: The LORD says he will send a messenger who will prepare the way before him. The messenger is also called the messenger of the covenant, whom the people desire and who is said to be coming.

l: sons of Levi, The Book of Malachi
s: offer offerings in righteousness [after being purified] The sons of Levi will be purified and refined like gold and silver by the LORD, who sits as a refiner and purifier. As a result they will offer offerings to the LORD in righteousness.

l: wrongdoers (sorcerers, adulterers, perjurers, oppressors), The Book of Malachi
s: The LORD says he will come near in judgment and be a swift witness against sorcerers, adulterers, and perjurers. The same judgment falls on those who oppress the hireling in his wages, the widow, and the fatherless, who deprive the foreigner of justice, and who do not fear him.

l: tithes and offerings, The Book of Malachi
s: Tithes and offerings are withheld from the LORD of Armies, which he calls robbery bringing a curse on the nation. He commands the whole tithe be brought to the storehouse, promising blessing, rebuke of the devourer, and restored pleasantness of Judah and Jerusalem's offering.

l: proud and wicked people, The Book of Malachi
s: The proud and all who work wickedness become stubble; the coming day burns them up, leaving neither root nor branch, and they end as ashes trodden beneath the feet of those who fear the LORD's name.

l: those who fear the LORD's name, The Book of Malachi
s: Those who fear the LORD's name are a faithful group who spoke with one another and honored him. The LORD listened, and a book of memory was written before him for them. He claims them as his own possession and will spare them as a father spares a serving son. On the coming day, the sun of righteousness will arise with healing, they will leap like calves, and they will tread down the wicked into ashes.

l: day of the LORD's coming, The Book of Malachi
s: The day of the LORD's coming is a great and terrible day of judgment and purification. In Chapter 3, no one can easily endure it, as he is like refiner's fire and launderers' soap, purifying the sons of Levi, judging wrongdoers, and claiming those who fear him. In Chapter 4, it burns like a furnace, consuming the proud and wicked to ashes beneath the righteous, with Elijah sent beforehand.

l: Elijah, The Book of Malachi
s: Elijah is a prophet promised to be sent by the LORD before the great and terrible day of the LORD, turning fathers' and children's hearts toward each other so the earth avoids being struck with a curse.
